### What this lab is for

A shorter exposure time reduces how far a moving subject travels while the shutter is open. This lab makes that sentence measurable: one subject, five shutter durations, and a log that predicts which frames will look sharp at the size you intend to show them. The idea is taught in the [capture module](#/module/photo-m01).

### What you need

- A camera that lets you set the shutter duration yourself.
- A subject that moves at a steady speed across the frame, such as a cyclist on a flat path.
- The downloaded log template, or paper with the same five columns.

### Steps

1. Estimate the subject's speed. A cyclist covering 50 metres in 10 seconds travels at 5 metres per second.
2. Before shooting, fill the _movement_ column: speed multiplied by the shutter duration.
3. Photograph the subject at each duration, keeping the aperture and the light as constant as you can.
4. View each frame at the size you intend to show it and mark whether the blur is visible.
5. Compare each prediction with what you marked.

### A worked log

| Shutter (s) | Speed (m/s) | Movement during exposure | Predicted  | Observed at phone size |
| ----------- | ----------- | ------------------------ | ---------- | ---------------------- |
| 1/1000      | 5           | 5 mm                     | sharp      | sharp                  |
| 1/250       | 5           | 20 mm                    | sharp      | sharp                  |
| 1/125       | 5           | 40 mm                    | borderline | sharp                  |
| 1/60        | 5           | about 83 mm              | blurred    | wheels blurred         |
| 1/30        | 5           | about 167 mm             | blurred    | whole rider blurred    |

The 1/125 row is the useful one. The prediction said borderline and, at phone size, the frame looked sharp. A large print of the same frame could show the blur, which is why the viewing size belongs in the log.

### What the log does not show

Camera shake and missed focus also soften a frame. The log controls neither, so a soft frame at 1/1000 s points to one of them rather than to subject motion.
